documents.abstract: Background: AI systems are increasingly deployed to support mental health clinicians, yet real-world evidence remains limited. In crisis counseling, where clients often seek human connection, understanding whether AI augmentation preserves or undermines meaningful human engagement is essential. Methods: In a mixed-methods study of a counselor-facing AI copilot on a WhatsApp-based crisis hotline in India (Mar.-Oct. 2025), counselors could request, edit, and send AI messages. We analyzed 20 interviews, 8 shadowing sessions, 56 survey responses, and edits in 27,778 copilot messages from 108 counselors via thematic analysis (Technology Acceptance Model 2, plus inductive coding of emergent factors), and survey statistics. Results: Counselors reported high copilot acceptance (survey): 98.2% found it helpful; 89.3% likely to continue use; 80.4% reported efficiency gains. Interviews highlighted sentence scaffolding, empathetic phrasing, stress reduction, catching missed details, and efficiency. Barriers (survey) included repetitive outputs (23.2%), lack of context (17.9%), and authenticity concerns (10.7%). While 69.6% (survey) reported skill enhancement, interviews surfaced skill atrophy concerns. Counselors frequently accepted copilot suggestions, editing to remove questions, adjust tone, or personalize style. Conclusion: In one of the largest real-world deployments of a counselor-facing mental health AI copilot, counselors reported reduced cognitive load, empathetic communication, and greater efficiency, alongside concerns about skill atrophy, authenticity, and over-reliance. In settings like crisis counseling where clients seek human connection, AI tools must balance operational support with preserving clinical skill and genuine therapeutic engagement. Designs soliciting approval or editing of complete drafts may overweight efficiency at the expense of sustained human engagement.

documents.abstract: As higher education increasingly adopts transdisciplinary frameworks to address complex societal challenges, cultivating students’ higher-order thinking (HOT) skills has become a key educational goal. These cognitive processes are essential in Human Factors Engineering (HFE), which requires students to address wicked problems inherent in transdisciplinary human-technology systems. However, traditional HFE curricula often emphasise rote memorisation of scientific theories. Meanwhile, the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has altered how students engage with academic content by enabling instant access to AI-generated responses. Despite increasing interest in AI-assisted learning, empirical evidence examining LLMs as co-creative partners in activities designed to support HOT remains limited. This quasi-experimental study compares two cohorts in an undergraduate HFE course, in which students either generated exam questions independently or co-created questions with an LLM. A total of 166 multiple-choice questions were collected and classified according to Bloom’s Taxonomy by two independent raters. Results indicate that the LLM-collaboration group produced a significantly higher proportion of higher-order questions. Among student-level factors, the number of student-AI dialogue turns was associated with question cognitive level, whereas self-reported AI usage frequency, metacognitive awareness and prior AI experience were not. Additionally, whether students adopted the AI’s suggested question or wrote their own after the dialogue did not affect question cognitive level. An exploratory analysis suggested that the number of turns in which students critically engaged with AI outputs was marginally associated with higher question cognitive level. These findings highlight the potential value of student-AI dialogue logs as a complementary source of assessment evidence.

Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.

We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

General large language models (LLMs) often have limited reliability when addressing specialized bridge pavement maintenance tasks. This study proposes Bridge-RoadLM, a domain-adapted framework for preliminary bridge pavement maintenance support. We developed an automated data engineering pipeline to construct the Bridge-Road Corpus, comprising 10,000 instruction-following samples derived from authoritative specifications and technical documents. Using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA), representative Qwen, DeepSeek, LLaMA, and Gemma models were adapted to bridge pavement maintenance tasks. A multilevel evaluation framework was established, including automated linguistic metrics, a 500-question expert-validated test bank, and a blinded multiengineer evaluation of open-ended inspection-report-style cases. Results show improved controlled task performance for several fine-tuned models, and the strongest improvement was for Qwen3-8B. Its accuracy in pavement defect diagnosis increased from 45.0% to 81.0%, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals of 35.6%–54.8% and 72.2%–87.5%, respectively. Its accuracy in bridge monitoring and maintenance increased from 25.0% to 75.0%, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals of 17.5%–34.3% and 65.7%–82.5%, respectively. In the blinded open-ended evaluation, six engineers with 10–17 years of professional experience scored anonymized model outputs using five predefined criteria: correctness, completeness, traceability, hallucination control, and safety. Qwen3-8B achieved the highest average score among the nine evaluated models. The results also show that fine-tuning effects varied across model families, indicating that domain-specific PEFT does not uniformly improve all LLMs. Overall, this study provides a specification-based instruction corpus and a controlled evaluation workflow for adapting locally deployable LLMs to bridge pavement maintenance, supporting preliminary specification referencing, defect interpretation, and draft-level maintenance-plan preparation within a human-in-the-loop workflow.

Complex 3D environments like Blender present a steep learning curve for novices, where topological errors often remain hidden until the final stages of a project. From a Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) perspective, supporting these users means moving away from static tutorials and toward active, real-time guidance. To explore this, we introduce “Learn & Fix,” a functional prototype Blender add-on with a rule-based architecture that detects mesh flaws in real time and helps new users by explaining their mistakes. We conducted a formative usability pilot study (N = 8) with absolute beginner users (less than 20 h of use) to evaluate interface discoverability, perceived usefulness, and interaction friction. Questionnaire responses highlighted an onboarding discoverability issue, as testers struggled to start the add-on in Blender’s native UI. User feedback indicates that in-viewport validation helps learners spot structural errors early. The design of an educational add-on must balance native UI integration with clear visibility.

documents.abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

Objectives: The CARDIO-ML-ED dataset was collected to address the critical shortage of publicly available cardiovascular databases that integrate electrocardiogram (ECG) imagery with comprehensive clinical metadata. Existing ECG repositories lack detailed patient-level information such as laboratory results, vital signs, and medical history—factors essential for developing clinically meaningful machine learning models. We aimed to create a curated, well-labelled, multimodal resource that supports research in automated ECG interpretation, multimodal fusion, and exploratory clinical phenotyping, while promoting reproducibility and innovation in artificial intelligence (AI) driven cardiovascular care. Data description: The CARDIO-ML-ED dataset comprises two complementary components: (1) structured clinical metadata for 582 subjects, and (2) a curated subset of 408 high-resolution ECG images derived from paper-based records digitized through standardized scanning, normalization, cropping, quality filtering, and noise reduction. The dataset includes 82 clinical features per subject—covering demographics, vital signs, laboratory tests (complete blood count, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, inflammatory markers, arterial blood gases), and medical history. Diagnostic labels were independently assigned by a cardiologist and an emergency medicine physician, achieving substantial interrater agreement (Cohen's kappa = 0.82). This resource offers unique value through its dense integration of ECG data with clinical covariates, enabling multimodal fusion research, unsupervised clustering, imbalanced learning, and predictive analytics.

Objective Pakistan has broadened its medical and dental education sphere, yet apprehensions last about undergraduates’ competence, impact of regulation, international acknowledgment of qualifications and retention of the health workforce. This study explored multi stakeholder perspectives on training capacity, quality of education, governance, regulation and acknowledgment of health professions education in Pakistan, and identified prime reforms. Methodology: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted using hybrid focus group discussion held on 4 August 2026 as part of national Health and Education Summit Pakistan (HESP) 2026. Fourteen purposively sampled stakeholders participated in discussion guided by 16 semi structured questions. Data were analysed using Framework Method, and Health Policy Triangle was applied as an interpretive lens. Results Nine themes were identified across three domains. Educational quality and competence : undefined and unenforced competency standards; deficits in clinical training infrastructure; faculty development and continuous quality improvement; and cautious, purpose-specific integration of artificial intelligence. Governance, regulation and recognition : fragmented, input-oriented governance; private-sector representation and public–private imbalance; and international recognition and global alignment. Workforce and equity : equity in workforce planning; and workforce sustainability, security and dignity. Participants identified main barrier to reform is not in an absence of policy but in weak implementation, input based accreditation and poor coordination among regulatory bodies. Conclusion Stakeholders called for a shift from input based to outcome-based accreditation built on a nationally agreed definition of competence, a shared inter agency governance platform, documented clinical supervision and simulation, and workforce protection measures.

Airport operational environments generate complex emission matrices that pose severe occupational health hazards, particularly in developing nations lacking systematic surveillance frameworks. This study characterised air quality dynamics at Benin City Airport, Nigeria, and evaluated the associated respiratory health burden among personnel. A cross-sectional mixed-methods design was deployed, combining eight weeks of real-time microenvironmental monitoring (CO₂, PM₁₀, PM₂.₅) with an epidemiological survey across 129 eligible airport workers. Significant spatiotemporal variations were detected for particulate matter: the airside zone exhibited peak coarse particle concentrations (PM₁₀: 22.04 ± 0.94 µg/m³) during morning shifts and progressive fine particle accumulation (PM₂.₅) during afternoon shifts, tracking flight operational cycles. Gaseous CO₂ concentrations showed no significant spatial variations across monitoring sites. Respiratory symptom prevalence was high among workers, dominated by chronic cough (57.4%) and shortness of breath (24.0%). Multivariable logistic regression revealed an exposure-awareness paradox: personnel in high-exposure operational zones (Airside and Terminal Halls) experienced significantly higher respiratory morbidity despite reporting higher occupational safety knowledge. Unawareness of safe exposure limits was inversely associated with chronic cough (AOR = 0.38, p = 0.032). High and fluctuating particulate levels create continuous inhalation hazards for frontline personnel. Mitigating these chronic occupational risks requires optimising administrative controls, enforcing mandatory shift rotations, ensuring consistent personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance, and establishing routine environmental health surveillance frameworks.

documents.abstract: Background: Mental health care often requires clinicians to reason over patient journeys: longitudinal patterns of symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, behaviors, social context, and responses to care. Yet these journeys are rarely documented as readily available, explicit timelines. Clinically important temporal information is often embedded in unstructured discharge narratives, where events may be repeated, narrated out of order, or expressed through vague and relative time references. This makes temporal recovery difficult for clinicians and computational systems, and can limit the reliability of downstream summarization. Methods: We present CliniCIRCA, a multi-stage large language model (LLM) framework for Calendar-anchored, Imprecision-aware Reconstruction of Clinical Annals. CliniCIRCA decomposes patient-journey reconstruction into three stages: extracting atomic clinical events from raw discharge summaries, assigning calendar-grounded temporal labels with explicit uncertainty, and rendering the verified timeline as a date-grouped clinical summary. The framework is designed to make temporal reasoning inspectable rather than hidden inside a single summarization step. Results: From 14,882 MIMIC-III mental-health-coded admissions, we construct a benchmark of 52 discharge summaries on which CliniCIRCA produces 15,891 temporally tagged events. Following clinician-defined rubrics, human annotation with clinician adjudication corrects 629 errors, producing verified gold-standard timelines. These corrected timelines then drive a temporally grounded summarization stage that compresses each source 1.52 times into a date-grouped chronological record while preserving temporal labels and uncertainty. We further scale the framework to generate 1,000 silver-standard timelines and evaluate them as supervision for smaller open-weight models. Compared with zero- and few-shot prompting, instruction tuning generally improves five open-weight models across event extraction, temporal tagging, and summarization under both silver and clinician-verified evaluations. Conclusions: Auditable temporal reconstruction can serve as both a clinician-readable representation of complex mental health narratives and a reusable supervision source for smaller models. These findings suggest that intermediate, temporally grounded representations may help bridge clinical summarization, timeline generation, and scalable model adaptation, while preserving the need for expert adjudication in high-stakes clinical natural language processing (NLP).

documents.abstract: Continual learning plays a crucial role in enabling artificial intelligence systems to accumulate knowledge over time without overwriting previously acquired information. While this capability is essential for real-world applications, especially in clinical domains where data evolves continuously, most existing approaches are designed for natural image scenarios and struggle when applied to medical imaging tasks. Medical images exhibit high intra-class similarity, making fine-grained recognition difficult. Meanwhile, adapter-based tuning with pretrained Vision Transformers introduces task-agnostic inference challenges due to the lack of task identity at test time. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a continual learning framework tailored for medical imaging, which enhances training and inference in class-incremental settings. First, we introduce a prompt-guided adapter design that focuses the model’s representation capacity on subtle disease-specific differences, improving feature discrimination. Second, we encourage knowledge reuse by facilitating communication between task-specific adapters, allowing the model to build upon prior information. Finally, during testing, we employ a collaborative inference mechanism that dynamically integrates multiple adapters, enabling robust predictions without relying on task labels. Experiments on several public medical image datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance and substantially alleviates forgetting compared to existing methods.

documents.abstract: We present CompCert4Lean, a large-scale port of CompCert 3.17's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean, completed in approximately six weeks by one expert directing parallel LLM agents. Our migration workflow partitions the development along its dependencies, audits translated definitions and theorem statements before large-scale proof reconstruction, and then reconstructs proofs in parallel against stable interfaces. The resulting compiler covers typed CompCert C through x86-64 assembly, discharges all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms, and produces executable Linux binaries. The workflow enabled the expert to concentrate on organizing the work rather than supplying technical solutions. Of 1,071 human interactions, 88.8% concerned workflow and coordination, while only three supplied technical direction. Optimization campaigns further demonstrate the benefit of the Lean port for agent-driven verified development. Under matched budgets of 24 active hours, GPT-6-astra produced a Lean candidate with 11.7% lower generated-program runtime across 29 small-tests programs, compared with 2.3% lower for its Rocq candidate, both relative to original CompCert 3.17 and while preserving the end-to-end correctness theorem. These results show that parallel LLM agents can support large-scale migration with limited human technical direction and subsequently improve the migrated compiler while retaining its formal guarantees.

Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation. It also reduces peak GPU memory by about 59\% at a sequence length of 2048 while retaining the sequence-length scaling behaviour of zeroth-order training.

Smartphones have repeatedly been proposed as companion input devices for head-mounted augmented reality (AR), but their usefulness depends on how the phone’s native interaction properties map onto the AR task. We present ControlAR, a prototype connecting an iPhone to a Magic Leap One through Bluetooth Low Energy and contrast two deliberately different mappings: direct text entry using the standard iOS keyboard and indirect spatial selection using a relative touchscreen trackpad. In a within-subject study with 18 participants, both mappings were compared with the Magic Leap One controller. Smartphone text entry was substantially faster (65.42 vs. 221.37 s), more accurate (0.73% vs. 2.18% errors), and rated more usable (SUS 92.08 vs. 71.67). For pointer selection, the smartphone was faster overall (68.43 vs. 76.68 s), yet the Magic Leap controller received markedly higher usability ratings (SUS 88.89 vs. 65.97). Rather than proposing a new pointing metaphor, we empirically characterize two pragmatic smartphone-to-AR mappings: direct reuse of mature touchscreen input and repurposing touch as relative spatial control. The results expose a speed–usability dissociation for trackpad pointing and identify tactile confirmation, ergonomics, and pointer gain as concrete design concerns.

Crystal plasticity (CP) simulations are widely used to predict the mechanical behavior of polycrystalline metals, yet their routine application remains hindered by the substantial manual effort of configuring heterogeneous tools, orchestrating multi-step data pipelines, and calibrating constitutive parameters against experimental measurements. These bottlenecks impede productivity in systematic parameter studies, motivating growing interest in automated workflow solutions. This study presents CP-Agent , a harness-engineered LLM-based agent that autonomously executes complete CP modeling workflows from tasks specified in natural language. Operating under the ReAct paradigm, the agent reasons about tool selection and sequencing while delegating numerical search to established optimizers. The harness comprises a minimal system prompt, typed tool definitions, a dispatcher, and a safety-bounded iteration loop, encoding domain knowledge through tool schemas rather than hard-coded logic. CP-Agent is demonstrated on four case studies: calibrating four slip parameters of additively manufactured stainless steel 316L against tensile data; validating the workflow against published copper benchmarks, reproducing stress–strain and texture evolution; recovering the initial crystallographic texture of copper, where the agent correctly identifies a diffuse initial texture; and reproducing the multi-pass rolling texture evolution of a Mg-Zn-Ca alloy, where the agent chains five deformation passes and recovers the experimentally observed weakened, split basal texture. In all cases, the agent inferred the correct execution sequence from the task statement, robustly across repeated runs, and delivered physically interpretable results. This work establishes harness engineering as a systematic approach to automating CP modeling workflows while maintaining physical interpretability and auditability through visible reasoning traces.

Background Voice-based depression screening is commercializing rapidly, yet whether voice biomarkers generalize across clinical settings is largely untested. Generalization is usually framed as a question about populations, but it is also a question about the outcome instrument a model is scored against, an effect confounded with other between-study differences in the literature. Objective We tested whether depression voice biomarkers transfer between perinatal and general-psychiatric speech in both directions under strict leakage control and whether transfer depends on the screening instrument. Methods In a cross-sectional, online US study, 390 pregnant participants at a mean of 22 (SD 1) weeks’ gestation (analytical sample n=316) participated in 446 sessions; each participant provided 4 voice recordings and completed the modified 8-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) and modified 9-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (mEPDS-9). We extracted 375 acoustic descriptors and 330-dimensional Population Dynamics Foundation Model community-health embeddings. Discrimination area under the curve (AUC) was assessed under leakage-controlled cross-validation, with feature and classifier selection inside training folds only and a permutation negative-control harness, across a prespecified grid of 4 speech tasks×4 outcome definitions. The prenatal-trained model was applied to 2 general-psychiatric corpora (Distress Analysis Interview Corpus–Wizard-of-Oz, n=189; Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, n=219) under pure held-out inference, and the open-source Kintsugi Depression/Anxiety Model (DAM), trained on 35,000 individuals, was applied to all 3 cohorts without refitting, with Benjamini-Hochberg multiplicity control. Results In the prenatal cohort, the preregistered outcome was at chance (AUC 0.494, 95% CI 0.431-0.560); no cell in the 16-cell grid survived adjustment under either modeling paradigm. The prenatal-trained model did not transfer to either general-psychiatric corpus (AUCs 0.505 and 0.478). Reverse transfer depended on the screening instrument. The DAM reached an AUC of 0.706 to 0.708 on general-psychiatric speech. In the same participants, it performed at chance against the PHQ-8 (AUC 0.510, 95% CI 0.411-0.609) but discriminated against the mEPDS-9 (AUC 0.645, 95% CI 0.541-0.744), a paired difference of 0.135 (95% CI 0.019-0.248; unadjusted post hoc P =0.02). Exploratory item-level analysis suggests a mechanism: the DAM tracked affective-distress items (crying r =0.26, sadness r =0.21, and overwhelmed r =0.20) but not somatic PHQ-8 items; only crying survived adjustment across 17 tests. Transfer varied by elicitation task (pregnancy narrative 0.653, 95% CI 0.550-0.753; open-ended speech 0.597, 95% CI 0.486-0.699; scripted reading 0.544, 95% CI 0.434-0.651), though these were not formally compared. Conclusions Cross-domain comparison showed a compound shift: population, elicitation task, and outcome instrument differed together, while only the instrument could be varied on its own. Whether a depression voice biomarker transfers may depend not only on the population but also on whether the outcome instrument captures what the model can detect. Validation should state the population, elicitation task, and outcome instrument together; a tool validated against one instrument should not be assumed to work against another.

documents.abstract: Assessment feedback in higher education provides fine-grained evidence about students’ specific errors but remains underutilized as a data source for teaching improvement. This study proposes a method based on a large language model (LLM) that transforms unstructured feedback into curriculum-aligned error analysis in three steps, deriving an error taxonomy from the feedback, mapping each piece to curriculum content by retrieval-augmented generation, and aggregating the annotations into error patterns with quantified cohort coverage. The method was applied to 6072 pieces of feedback across four cohorts (2022–2025) of an undergraduate engineering course. The feedback resolved into recurring, curriculum-aligned error patterns, dominated by missing content and justification, clustered in identifiable modules and weeks, and more than half recurring across cohorts. The resulting annotations achieved 89.1% agreement with human judgment, substantially higher than the 74.7% obtained when an expert-designed taxonomy was applied to the same data. In a focus group, the teaching team confirmed the patterns against their marking experience, proposed course revisions from them, and set the bound that they serve as a reference and not as a direct measure of teaching quality. The study reports a process account of this team’s use of curriculum-aligned error analytics, built on sensemaking and pedagogical response. The analysis turns feedback written for students into evidence on the teaching that preceded it, by which a teaching team can check the alignment between intended outcomes, teaching, and assessment in students’ actual work, reflect on its own practice, and improve its teaching across cohorts.

These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

The respectful disposal of damaged Quranic texts presents a crucial socio-religious and environmental management issue for Islamic religious authorities. In Malaysia, the DepartmenThe respectful disposal of damaged Quranic texts presents a crucial socio-religious and environmental management issue for Islamic religious authorities. In Malaysia, the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia (JAKIM) guidelines specify controlled burning as an approved method. However, existing disposal incinerators operated by state authorities, such as Jabatan Agama Islam Melaka (JAIM), face significant operational issues, including excessive toxic smoke emissions, ergonomic limitations, ash loss due to wind scattering, and performance degradation from 300 kg/day to 150 kg/day after two years. This study presents the design, Finite Element Analysis (FEA), and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulation of a redesigned 304 stainless steel Al-Quran disposal incinerator. Concept selection using the Pugh Matrix identified an optimized design incorporating an air blower, smoke filter, dust compartment, and hydraulic lift table. CFD simulations demonstrate that forced aeration elevates internal combustion temperature from 617 °C (blower off) to 1,725 °C (blower on), increasing thermal efficiency and reducing total burning time for 150 kg of paper to under 24 hours. Static FEA using the Von Mises Yield Criterion indicates that while the structure safely supports 300 kg under ambient conditions (FOS = 1.0), thermal stresses at 1,725 °C limit the safe structural payload to 150 kg (FOS = 1.1). To mitigate high-temperature sensitization (425–870 °C) and intergranular corrosion, protective enamel or Ni-Cr composite coatings are evaluated. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make introductory programming tasks easier to complete, but a working program is not evidence of durable learning. This conceptual-theoretical paper integrates research on cognitive load, metacognition, self-explanation, productive failure, appropriate reliance on automation, and recent studies of AI-assisted programming to propose a five-phase cognitive-scaffolding framework. Learners first make an unaided attempt, request bounded assistance, verify the response against requirements and independently designed tests, explain the mechanism and calibrate confidence, and then complete a related transfer task as support fades. AI literacy, ethical disclosure, privacy, and instructor orchestration operate across all phases. The framework identifies process evidence that remains inspectable when generated code is available, including problem representations, hypotheses, verification records, explanations, confidence judgments, and unaided transfer. It also states six testable propositions and an evaluation blueprint for introductory programming courses. The contribution is a bounded design logic, not a claim that the sequence has already been validated: GenAI should reduce avoidable burden while leaving consequential decisions, checks, and explanations with the learner.

documents.abstract: The development of students’ visual–spatial reasoning is a persistent challenge in geometry learning, where abstract representations and spatial transformations require high levels of cognitive engagement. Although flipped learning has been widely implemented to promote active learning, its effectiveness largely depends on the quality of instructional design and pedagogical support provided during in-class activities. This study investigates how metacognitive scaffolding can be intentionally designed and embedded within flipped learning to enhance students’ visual–spatial reasoning. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed in secondary geometry instruction involving 62 students assigned to experimental and control groups. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-tests of visual–spatial reasoning, while qualitative data were obtained from classroom observations and semi-structured teacher interviews. The results indicate that students who experienced metacognitive scaffolding within a flipped learning environment demonstrated significantly greater gains in visual–spatial reasoning than those in a conventional flipped classroom, with a large effect size. Qualitative findings further reveal that scaffolding prompts supported students’ planning, monitoring, and reflective evaluation during problem-solving activities. Overall, the findings suggest that flipped learning environments become more cognitively productive when structured metacognitive scaffolding is deliberately incorporated into the learning design.

Opening a vehicle fuel cap can be challenging for individuals experiencing reduced hand strength, impaired motor control, or upper-limb functional limitations because the task requires secure gripping and rotational force. This preliminary study aimed to develop and evaluate 3D-printed assistive-tool concepts for vehicle fuel-cap manipulation using a user-centred approach involving end users and occupational therapy (OT) professionals. Four initial design concepts were developed, of which two prototypes were selected for user evaluation. The prototypes were demonstrated with support from the Rehabilitation Department of Hospital Taiping and evaluated using a structured five-point Likert-scale instrument. Eleven end-user respondents and four OT professionals participated in the evaluation. End users assessed ease of use, ergonomics, effectiveness, safety, and user satisfaction, while OT professionals assessed clinical suitability, ergonomics, safety, functional benefit, and potential for practical application. The end-user group produced overall mean scores of 3.96 for Design 1 and 4.04 for Design 2, indicating generally favourable perceptions of both prototypes and a marginally higher rating for Design 2. OT professionals provided a higher overall rating for Design 1 (5.00) than Design 2 (3.63). Qualitative feedback highlighted the need for improved hand support, grip security, handle configuration, and fuel-cap engagement. The differing evaluations between end users and OT professionals suggest that stakeholder perspectives should be considered concurrently during early-stage assistive-device development. The findings support the feasibility of using 3D printing to rapidly develop task-specific assistive-tool prototypes, while the current results should be interpreted as preliminary rather than evidence of clinical effectiveness. Future work should incorporate objective measurements of grip force, rotational torque, task completion time, mechanical durability, and compatibility with different fuel-cap geometries.

documents.abstract: Conventional desks are designed around fixed dimensions and lower structural elements that can hinder frontal approach, reach, and comfortable posture for wheelchair users, limiting their participation in study and work activities. This study aimed to develop a modular and accessible desk concept for wheelchair users through Design Thinking and User-Centered Design. An applied, mixed-methods, descriptive-propositive approach was followed, structured in the five phases of Design Thinking: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. In the empathize phase, a questionnaire with two five-point Likert scales (perceived difficulty and importance of desk features) was administered to ten people, six wheelchair users and four non-users, selected through non-probability sampling. Data were analyzed descriptively, and internal consistency was estimated with Cronbach’s alpha. Both scales showed high internal consistency (α = 0.955 and 0.929). The greatest difficulties were plugging in devices and maintaining posture during long periods, while height adjustment, removable storage modules, and ample work surface were the most valued features (mean = 4.20). These findings informed a design brief, a conceptual sketch, and a three-dimensional model of an L-shaped desk with adjustable height, removable storage modules, device charging, and open space for frontal approach. The project is currently at the three-dimensional modeling stage; a physical prototype has not been built, and usability, stability, and ergonomic tests with users remain pending. Because of the small sample and the preliminary nature of the instrument, the results are exploratory and support the relevance of the proposed features rather than confirming the effectiveness of the desk. Future work will build the prototype and evaluate it with a larger group of wheelchair users.

documents.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulas feature complex chemical compositions, and their HPLC quality control method development is time-consuming and experience-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) provide a promising strategy for intelligently assisting analytical method construction. Taking the Eczema External Wash Formula as the research object, this work constructed a human-machine collaborative workflow involving intelligent recommendation, experimental validation and iterative optimization for HPLC method development. Among five prompt strategies tested, expert-role setting with structured reasoning performed best. After inputting formula information, the LLM proposed five chromatographic schemes. Through experimental screening and optimization, the final HPLC method used a SunShell C18 column, mobile phase of 0.1% aqueous formic acid-acetonitrile for gradient elution, with seven markers separated within 55 min. Twenty components were characterized by LC-MS. The validated method exhibited satisfactory linearity, precision, repeatability, stability and recovery. This indicates LLMs can reduce the workload of chromatographic condition exploration and boost the development efficiency of TCM formula analytical methods, supporting intelligent TCM quality control.

Introduction Society 5.0 integrates advanced digital technologies with human-centered work systems, yet its implications for sustainable employee performance remain underexplored. Drawing on Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examines the relationship between Society 5.0 enablement intensity (S5EI) and sustainable human performance through autonomous motivation and emotional exhaustion, considering human-centric governance capability as a moderator. Methods The study employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyse data collected from 519 employees working in digitally intensive sectors in India. Results The findings indicate that S5EI is positively associated with sustainable human performance, primarily through autonomous motivation. Emotional exhaustion partially offsets this positive effect through competitive mediation. Human-centric governance capability strengthens the relationship between autonomous motivation and sustainable human performance but does not significantly buffer the negative effect of emotional exhaustion. Discussion The findings conceptualize digital enablement as a dual-valence work condition that simultaneously strengthens autonomy-based motivation and increases digital demands, integrating Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of participatory digital governance, workload management, and employee recovery measures for supporting sustainable human performance.

Background: Digital Eye Strain (DES) is a common ocular and visual complaint associated with prolonged use of digital devices. The widespread move to online learning and remote work has markedly increased screen exposure, which may place students and remote workers at greater risk. This systematic …

In an education increasingly mediated by smart technologies, it is essential that nursing students maintain critical thinking and autonomous clinical judgment. Digital literacy goes beyond technical expertise, incorporating an ethical, conscious, and contextualized analysis of the social, political, and epistemological impacts of artificial intelligence. This competence prevents the uncritical use of digital tools and fosters an understanding of their mechanisms, risks, and limitations, including biases and misinformation. In the context of nursing, this approach ensures that technology complements human judgment without compromising safety and person-centered care. Thus, training should be guided by ethical principles, critical reflection, and professional responsibility, preparing future nurses for an increasingly complex and digital clinical landscape. The study participants are nursing students in a clinical teaching setting. The review will follow the JBI methodology and reporting according to PRISMA-ScR. The databases to be searched include CINAHL Plus Complete, MEDLINE Complete Plus, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by unpublished literature in the ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Citation Index (via Web of Science) and RCAAP. Studies in Portuguese, English, and Spanish will be included. Two independent reviewers will perform the analysis, extraction, and synthesis of data using the Rayyan platform. The results will be presented narratively, with tables or figures.

Organizations navigating digital transformation face persistent challenges integrating social and technical elements to support innovation and worker wellbeing. Despite increasing workforce participation, women remain underrepresented in senior leadership roles that shape how this integration occurs, leaving perspectives shaped by gendered organizational experience underexplored within digital transformation research. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with sixteen senior women leaders across Australian organizations, this study applies socio‐technical systems theory and a gender‐informed leadership perspective to examine how these leaders understood and navigated the relationship between technical and social domains during digital transformation. Participants treated technical and social considerations as mutually constitutive, enacting their integration through communication, employee participation, human‐centered work design, capability development and ongoing adaptation. Psychosocial safety emerged across technical, social and integration‐focused accounts as a system‐level condition implicated in this process. Together, these findings provide an empirical account of human‐centric transformation within Industry 5.0 and extend socio‐technical systems theory by conceptualizing integration as an enacted process through which technical and social considerations continually shape one another. A gender‐informed analysis further demonstrates the value of gendered organizational experience for understanding how socio‐technical integration is accomplished in practice.

Orbital data centers could enable large-scale AI inference, but efficiently serving a frontier language model to many users may require several compute satellites to cooperate over optical links. While disaggregated inference, which splits large language model (LLM) serving across machines, is well established in terrestrial data centers, its viability under the unique constraints of orbital deployments remains an open question. This article investigates how link capacity and satellite separation affect two types of disaggregated LLM serving, in both compact satellite formations and distributed constellations. Prefill-decode disaggregation (PDD) migrates a large KV cache once per request, while attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) exchanges small activations at every mixture-of-experts layer for every generated token. The two respond to distance in different ways. PDD is limited mainly by link capacity and, with fast enough links, tolerates separations of up to a thousand kilometers. AFD is limited mainly by propagation delay, which accumulates layer by layer and forces attention and expert instances within about a kilometer of each other. Based on these results, we propose a hierarchical orbital inference architecture and provide network design guidelines for future orbital data centers, including the role of ground access latency.

Introdução: O sector de contact center constitui um dos pilares da economia digital, mas impõe aos seus colaboradores riscos ergonómicos e psicossociais elevados, decorrentes da imobilidade prolongada, da repetitividade gestual e da pressão por indicadores de desempenho. Na empresa Ucall, em Angola, a incidência de Distúrbios Musculoesqueléticos Relacionados ao Trabalho (DORT) constitui um desafio relevante à saúde ocupacional. Objetivo: Analisar a prevalência dos distúrbios musculoesqueléticos e discutir estratégias de prevenção fisioterapêutica em colaboradores de contact center na empresa Ucall, no primeiro semestre de 2025. Metodologia: Estudo descritivo, de abordagem mista (quantitativa e qualitativa) e corte transversal, realizado na empresa Ucall (Talatona, Luanda). A amostra, não probabilística e por conveniência, foi composta por 22 colaboradores de uma população de 80. Os dados foram recolhidos remotamente via Google Forms, com recurso ao Questionário Nórdico de Sintomas Osteomusculares (QNSO) e à Escala Visual Analógica (EVA). Resultados: Identificou-se um paradoxo estrutural: embora 72,7% dos postos de trabalho disponham de cadeiras com ajuste técnico, apenas uma minoria dos colaboradores adota posturas adequadas. A coluna lombar (31,8%) e a região dorsal (18,2%) concentraram a maior prevalência de queixas, com níveis médios de dor entre 6 e 8 na escala EVA em quase metade da amostra. A pressão por metas influenciou a tensão muscular em 77,3% dos inquiridos, e 59,1% classificaram as pausas laborais como apenas ligeiramente satisfatórias. Conclusões: A prevalência elevada de DORT na empresa Ucall exige uma estratégia multidimensional de prevenção fisioterapêutica, que integre ergonomia física, gestão da carga mental e educação postural desde a admissão, consolidando a fisioterapia ocupacional como elemento estratégico para a sustentabilidade da saúde no trabalho. Palavras-chave: Distúrbios Musculoesqueléticos; Prevalência; Contact Center; Fisioterapia Ocupacional; Ucall; Angola. ABSTRACT Introduction: The contact center sector is a pillar of the digital economy, but it exposes employees to elevated ergonomic and psychosocial risks arising from prolonged immobility, repetitiveness, and pressure related to performance indicators. At the Ucall company, in Angola, the incidence of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WRMSD) constitutes a relevant occupational health challenge. Objective: To analyze the prevalence of musculoskeletal disorders and to discuss physiotherapeutic prevention strategies among contact center employees at the Ucall company, in the first semester of 2025. Methods: A descriptive study with a mixed quantitative-qualitative approach and a cross-sectional design was conducted at the Ucall company (Talatona, Luanda). The non-probabilistic, convenience sample consisted of 22 employees drawn from a population of 80. Data were collected remotely via Google Forms, using the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ) and the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS). Results: A structural paradox was identified: although 72.7% of workstations were equipped with technically adjustable chairs, only a minority of employees adopted adequate posture. The lumbar spine (31.8%) and thoracic region (18.2%) concentrated the highest prevalence of complaints, with mean pain levels between 6 and 8 on the VAS scale in nearly half of the sample. Pressure for targets influenced muscular tension in 77.3% of respondents, and 59.1% rated work breaks as only slightly satisfactory. Conclusions: The high prevalence of WRMSD at Ucall requires a multidimensional physiotherapeutic prevention strategy integrating physical ergonomics, mental workload management, and postural education from onboarding, consolidating occupational physiotherapy as a strategic element for workplace health sustainability. documents.abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Within the golden 72 h after an earthquake, the rapid generation of emergency thematic maps is critical for disaster assessment and rescue decision-making, yet it faces core challenges such as the difficulty of reusing experience from historical earthquakes and the weak association among multi-source heterogeneous data. The spatial hallucination inherent in conventional spatial RAG systems can further mislead situational awareness of the affected region and increase decision risk. To address these issues, this paper proposes an adaptive dynamic thematic map generation method that fuses LLMs with Graph RAG for earthquake emergency scenarios. At the knowledge reconstruction level, a dual-channel association constraint mechanism over spatial and semantic channels is designed to link base geographic data, emergency resources, and historical cases across modalities, thereby constructing a directed heterogeneous event-region-resource spatial knowledge graph and achieving spatially grounded semantic consolidation of heterogeneous spatiotemporal multi-source data in emergency scenarios. At the retrieval and reasoning level, asymmetric query rewriting and multi-dimensional parallel recall over graph topology are introduced together with causal constraints of earthquake-triggered spatiotemporal propagation and proactive circuit breaking, which upgrades the text matching of conventional RAG to multi-hop spatiotemporal causal reasoning over the entire cross-domain chain of earthquake emergency response, suppresses spatial hallucination at the source of spatial decision making, and ensures the rigor of historical case reuse. At the collaborative mapping level, a multi-dimensional text fusion model of evolutionary evidence chains is constructed, which converts the discrete reasoning results of the LLM into standardized structured semantics and realizes mechanism-driven mapping of disaster semantics such as seismic intensity and lifeline engineering damage onto emergency thematic map layers. In addition, in-memory and distributed multi-level caching strategies are introduced to reduce the computational response latency when massive data floods in after strong earthquakes. Experiments on real earthquakes such as the Lushan and Luding events show that the proposed method raises the layer match rate to 0.791 (versus 0.295 for the strongest baseline), achieves the best layer-set F1 (0.252), reduces the in-window viewport-center displacement to 21.2 km, and attains a blind-judged semantic accuracy of 0.429 over the full 200-query set (0.881 on in-window queries) against 0.00 for all baselines, while a spatially filtered hybrid baseline reaches only 0.068. Driven by a lightweight 7B model, the cold-start generation of a single thematic map takes only 0.83 min, and the dynamic viewport refresh is kept within 12 s when the cache is activated, which meets the time window requirement for rapid post-earthquake map production. Given the moderate overall semantic accuracy and the disclosed out-of-graph coverage boundary, the method is positioned as an efficient and verifiable decision-support solution whose outputs still require human verification, rather than as a fully autonomous cartographic product.

After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

This study investigated the effect of facilitated Problem-Based Learning (PBL) on intrinsic and extrinsic motivation among nursing students in North-East Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test control group design was adopted. The population comprised 1,065 ND II nursing students from six Colleges of Nursing Science in North-East Nigeria, from which 200 students were selected using a multi-stage sampling procedure. The sample consisted of 100 students in the experimental group exposed to facilitated PBL and 100 students in the control group taught using conventional lecture-based instruction. Data were collected using a 28-item Academic Motivation Questionnaire (AMQ). The instrument demonstrated satisfactory reliability with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.84. The experimental group participated in a six-week facilitated PBL intervention involving nursing-related case scenarios, guided questioning, collaborative learning, feedback, and self-directed learning activities. Data were analyzed using means, standard deviations, and t-tests at the 0.05 level of significance. Finding showed that the experimental group recorded an increase in mean intrinsic-motivation scores from 26.30 at pre-test to 50.30 at post-test, compared with an increase from 25.90 to 30.20 in the control group. A significant effect was also found on extrinsic motivation, with the experimental group recording a greater reduction in extrinsic motivation than the control group, t(198) = 8.72, p < .05. therefore, motivation also differed significantly between the facilitated PBL and lecture groups, t(198) = 14.02, p < .001. Furthermore, a significant difference was observed between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, t(198) = 6.85, p < .001. The study concluded that facilitated PBL is an effective instructional approach for strengthening intrinsic motivation and promoting more self-directed learning among nursing students. It was recommended that nursing institutions should integrate facilitated PBL into their programmes, train educators in effective PBL facilitation, provide adequate learning resources, and emphasize learning activities that foster students’ intrinsic motivation.

Considering that stroke is one of the main causes of physical disability worldwide, with more than 60% of survivors presenting residual motor impairment, and that conventional physical therapy imposes limitations on repetitiveness and adherence, the objective is to analyze the efficacy of virtual reality (VR) and gamification in the physical therapy rehabilitation of post-stroke patients, emphasizing motor function and treatment adherence. Therefore, a narrative/integrative literature review of a descriptive-analytical nature is carried out, with qualitative synthesis of evidence, performed in the BVS/LILACS, SciELO, PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar databases, with an adapted PICO strategy, DeCS/MeSH descriptors and free terms, between 2015 and 2025, in Portuguese and English, which resulted in the inclusion of 18 studies organized into two thematic axes. Thus, it is observed that VR, especially when associated with conventional physical therapy, promotes consistent benefits on upper limb motor function, balance, gait and coordination, with small to moderate effect sizes (SMD 0.32; 95% CI 0.08–0.56) and moderate to low certainty of evidence, and that gamification favors adherence and engagement by increasing intrinsic motivation, although the evidence for this outcome is scarcer and heterogeneous. This allows concluding that VR and gamification are promising and complementary resources to conventional physical therapy, with documented benefits on motor function and relevant potential for treatment adherence, and that Brazilian randomized clinical trials with standardized protocols and validated adherence measurement instruments are recommended.

We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents are entering administrative processes. This marks a shift from robotic process automation to intelligent automation and raises the question of what role people keep when systems process, analyze, and make decisions. The objective was to critically analyze the literature from 2020 to 2026 on the competencies that are transformed or emerging, and on research trends and gaps. A critical and integrative documentary study was carried out in Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, Redalyc, Dialnet, and Google Scholar. It included peer-reviewed studies in Spanish and English, which were analyzed with an extraction matrix and a thematic synthesis. Based on the reviewed literature, GenAI cuts writing time by up to 40% and raises productivity by 15%, especially among novices. However, greater trust in it reduces critical thinking. The emerging competencies are data analysis, digital and complex cognitive skills, decision-making, and continuous learning. Qualitative and short-term studies predominate. There are gaps in the quality of oversight, in Latin American contexts, SMEs, and the public sector, and in the development of expertise. The human role is shifting from execution to oversight and governance. It is effective only under adequate conditions and complying with a protocol is not enough.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This paper presents an analytical synthesis of contemporary research fronts in public relations (PR) scholarship, drawing on recent work in leading journals (Public Relations Review, Journal of Public Relations Research, Corporate Communications: An International Journal), agenda-setting signals from disciplinary bodies (ICA, IPR, PRSA), and 2025–2026 special-issue programs. Seven interrelated research fronts are identified: (a) artificial intelligence adoption, ethics, and disciplinary disruption; (b) disinformation, trust, and organizational resilience; (c) theoretical and methodological pluralism, including de-Westernization; (d) employee communication, advocacy, and internal activism; (e) crisis spillover and contagion; (f) measurement, evaluation, and predictive analytics; and (g) bibliometric self-mapping. The analysis argues that these fronts are shaped by three macro-level forces—technological disruption, epistemic diversification, and disciplinary self-examination—and that the intersections among them constitute the field’s most promising publication spaces. Drawing on recent empirical evidence, including a 277-agency survey of AI adoption across the Arab world (Koa et al., 2025), a longitudinal analysis of 630 fact-checks of disinformation targeting organizations in Spain (Rodríguez Fernández et al., 2026), and a dedicated special issue on crisis spillover (Laufer & Wang, 2024), the synthesis shows that the field’s most successful emerging work does not abandon established PR theory but redeploys it in new empirical territories. The paper concludes with a maturity–opportunity assessment and a strategic map of research gaps to guide manuscript positioning in Q1/Q2 outlets during the 2026–2027 publication cycle.
topics: News Media Framing and Political Communication

documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Digital transformation, remote and hybrid work, and the diffusion of artificial intelligence have made employee adaptability a critical organizational capability, yet research on its antecedents remains fragmented across psychology, information systems, and management. This study aims to synthesize evidence on the individual and organizational determinants of employee adaptability in the digital workplace. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and ABI/INFORM for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025, and findings were integrated through thematic synthesis. The review shows that adaptability is conceptualized as a multidimensional capability spanning cognitive, behavioral, and emotional responses to technological change. Individual determinants include dispositional traits, self-efficacy and digital competence, career adaptability, and attitudes toward change, whereas organizational determinants include leadership and change communication, psychological safety, training, job and technology design, and flexible work arrangements. The literature suggests that these determinants operate as interacting resources, with supportive organizational conditions amplifying individual capacity. An integrative framework and a research agenda emphasizing longitudinal, multilevel, and emerging-economy studies are proposed. The findings guide managers and human resource practitioners in designing workplaces that support adaptation.

Athletes are often at high risk of sudden and severe injury or illness during training sessions due to a lack of safety measures. Failure to monitor health conditions and vital signs during training can result in serious consequences for athletes. Currently, several devices in the market measure vital signs and provide them as raw data; however, they do not prioritize the athlete’s safety and often offer limited feedback on their health condition. Additionally, many of these devices lack ergonomic designs, which limit the athlete’s mobility. This wearable health monitoring device was designed to be both lightweight and cost-effective. It collects and tracks health metrics while providing real-time feedback to the user via an application to support the athlete’s safety. A key feature is the utilization of energy harvesting technology to power the system, which includes a heart rate sensor, core body temperature sensor, and sweat sensor. Furthermore, the acquired data are analyzed using a developed algorithm to detect abnormal and critical health conditions such as dehydration, overtraining syndrome, exertional heat illnesses, and heart attacks risk indicators. These critical data points, which exceed normal ranges, are classified into two alarm levels: Warning Level and Critical Level. Ultimately, the data are transmitted via Wi-Fi to a mobile application, which provides information about the athlete’s health status and guidance to ensure their safety.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials
Wireless Sensor Networks for Data Analysis

documents.abstract: Interactive virtual reality (VR) reduces acute pain, but the reasons it works are usually assumed rather than directly tested. VR experiences differ widely in how physically and cognitively demanding they are. It is therefore unclear whether relief comes mainly from physical activity or from cognitive engagement. In this study, 29 healthy adults were exposed to a controlled painful stimulus while experiencing one non-interactive baseline and three interactive VR tasks that varied in physical effort. After each trial, participants rated their pain relief, immersion, attention, and how active they felt. The three tasks did not differ in pain relief, despite differing in physical demand, which does not support physical exertion as the main factor. Participants’ ratings of immersion, attention, and activity combined into a single measure of engagement, and a Bayesian within-subject mediation analysis estimated that this engagement accounted for most of the pain relief. This held even when physical activity was excluded from the engagement measure, which points to cognitive engagement rather than physical effort. Individuals who engaged more deeply also tended to report greater pain relief. In this VR setup, pain relief was therefore associated mainly with cognitive engagement rather than physical activity. Because engagement was measured rather than manipulated, this pathway remains correlational. The results nonetheless suggest that VR pain applications should be designed for engagement rather than physical demand.
