documents.abstract: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

During flight test operations, distributed aircraft power systems are typically managed by human operators through centralized monitoring interfaces. Operators must balance system health, mission objectives, and safety margins under dynamically changing test conditions. However, existing systems are largely reactive and primarily provide fault alerts without predictive insight, which can delay timely intervention and increase operator cognitive workload. This paper proposes a human-AI collaborative decision framework for distributed aircraft power management in flight test environments. The framework integrates predictive health assessment, risk modeling, and strategy evaluation to support operator decision making. A lightweight prognostic mechanism continuously estimates the health risk of individual power cabinets using electrical and thermal indicators. Based on the predicted risk, the system identifies high-risk modules and recommends a small set of feasible power management strategies that balance risk mitigation and mission impact. Human operators remain responsible for final decision selection through a human-centered interface that visualizes system health and strategy options. A simulation-based experimental study using a Wizard-of-Oz platform compares conventional manual management with the proposed Human-AI decision support approach. Results show that the framework improves risk detection efficiency, increases decision accuracy, and reduces unnecessary load shedding. The findings demonstrate the potential of human-AI collaboration to enhance situational awareness and decision performance in safety-critical aircraft power management tasks.

The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational work has implications for employee collaboration, technological demands, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance. This study examines the relationships among leadership vision, employee-AI collaboration, techno-overload, AI overreliance, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance. Cross-sectional survey data from 424 respondents were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that leadership vision is positively associated with employee-AI collaboration and decision autonomy. Employee-AI collaboration is positively associated with AI overreliance, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance, while techno-overload is strongly associated with AI overreliance. Decision autonomy exhibits the strongest direct association with adaptive performance and a significant positive indirect role in the relationship between employee-AI collaboration and adaptive performance. In contrast, the hypothesized negative relationships of techno-overload and AI overreliance with decision autonomy are not supported, nor is the proposed indirect relationship between techno-overload and adaptive performance through decision autonomy. The findings distinguish collaborative AI engagement from reliance-related concerns and highlight the relevance of decision autonomy to employee adaptability. The study contributes to understanding the relationships among organizational leadership, AI-related work experiences, and adaptive performance, offering practical considerations for maintaining employee discretion and responsible AI use in AI-enabled workplaces.

Purpose This study aims to eliminate part-supply errors, reduce non-value-added labour, and improve ergonomic conditions in high-mix single-axis linear actuator assembly using the DMAIC methodology. Methods A DMAIC-based case study was conducted in a Vietnamese precision-component manufacturing plant. Pareto analysis, process observation, 4M Ishikawa diagrams, on-site verification, and cause-prioritization matrices identified three root causes from seven candidates. Five improvement solutions were implemented, including single-order kitting, a two-level tray conveyor, centralized automatic ball feeding, point-of-use parts storage, and barcode-based poka-yoke verification. Results Missing and incorrect parts accounted for 76% of assembly part defects, with an initial supply-error rate of 0.31%. Supply errors decreased from 6.33 per month to zero during the post-improvement verification month (p ≈ 0.0018). Ball insertion time decreased by 1.13 minutes per cycle, while non-value-added labour was reduced by 3,203 hours annually. The improvements generated annual savings of US$7,110 from a US$5,200 investment, achieving an 8.8-month payback period and a first-year return on investment of approximately 37%. Value : This study demonstrates a cost-effective, human-centred DMAIC approach integrating error-proofing, material-flow redesign, and ergonomic improvements to enhance assembly quality, operational efficiency, and sustainable manufacturing practices.

Background Adolescent girls in rural India face substantial barriers to mental healthcare, including restrictive gender norms, limited digital autonomy and a severe shortage of trained professionals. Digital mental health interventions offer scalable solutions but require contextual adaptation to achieve meaningful engagement. This study aims to identify multi-level barriers and co-produce a stakeholder-endorsed roadmap for adapting the Wysa application, an artificial intelligence-based conversational agent, and its implementation strategies for adolescent girls in rural Uttar Pradesh. It is a formative, pre-implementation intervention-adaptation study and constitutes the first work package of a five-year research programme. Methods and analysis This protocol describes a sequential, participatory mixed-methods study conducted across five districts of Uttar Pradesh, namely Bahraich, Barabanki, Hardoi, Lucknow and Sitapur, with a total sample ranging between 120–175 participants. Step 1 will comprise of 15 in-person participatory workshops with adolescent girls (n = 60–90), parents and guardians (n = 35–50) and community stakeholders (n = 25–35), supplemented by semi-structured interviews with a subset of adolescent girls, analysed thematically and mapped to the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behaviour (COM-B) model and the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) taxonomy. Step 2 will employ two rounds of Delphi survey (n = 24) to prioritise barriers and candidate strategies against the APEASE criteria. Step 3 will apply a modified nominal group technique (n = 18–24) to co-produce the final adaptation roadmap. Ethics and dissemination The protocol has been approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai (2026/51/E26005). Written informed consent, and parental consent with participant assent for minors, will be obtained. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed open-access journals, academic conferences and community-level platforms coordinated with the Lived Experience Advisory Group. Registration The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07595029) on 12th May 2026. The details can be found at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07595029.

Large language models can generate code based on natural language prompts, opening up new possibilities for users to customize software and extend its functionality. This paper proposes and implements Injectra, a general-purpose code injection and feature enhancement system for existing desktop clients, suitable for applications whose user interfaces are built using embedded browser engines (such as Electron) or system WebViews (such as Tauri). Injectra decouples the host integration logic from the upper-layer enhancement code. Combining both runtime integration and pre-launch bootstrap mechanisms, it injects JavaScript, HTML, and CSS into the application's internal Web runtime environment through a unified execution channel, thereby enabling modifications to interface rendering, adjustments to interactive behaviors, and client-side functionality extensions. The system uses a command-line interface (CLI) as a unified entry point, allowing external tools, AI agents, and MCP integration layers to reuse its injection and enhancement capabilities. We tested 38 desktop applications already installed on our macOS machine; code injection was successfully completed for all of them. We demonstrated the system's capability to extend functionality through various enhanced use cases and also successfully validated the Windows version. Based on Injectra, we further developed an LLM-powered enhancement tool driven by selection and annotation: users select interface objects within the original application and describe their modification requirements; the large language model then generates the enhancement code, which is injected, executed, and rendered by Injectra. The system's source code has now been released as open source: https://github.com/sqmw/injectra.

Digital transformation in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) requires contextual and character-oriented learning innovations. This qualitative library research aims to analyze the takhrij and matn of hadiths regarding intention and the obligation to seek knowledge, and formulates their integration into Project-Based Learning (PjBL). Tracing transmission chains, matn criticism, and pedagogical content analysis were employed. Results show that the hadith on intention (Sahih al-Bukhari No. 1) is authentic (muttafaq 'alaih), serving as an ethical foundation of sincerity, while the hadith on seeking knowledge (Sunan Ibn Majah No. 224) is hasan li ghairihi. Integrating these hadiths into PjBL yields three Islamic academic ethical pillars (al-ikhlas, al-itqan, al-'amal wa al-naf') that enhance students' intrinsic motivation, academic integrity, and social responsibility. This conceptual framework offers an accountable pedagogical innovation for IRE..

Tablet computers, and the iPad in particular, have been introduced into secondary schools on a large scale, often through one-to-one programmes justified by claims that portable, touch-based devices will make science learning more engaging, more authentic and more effective. Empirical support for such claims is uneven, and the theoretical reasons why an iPad-assisted activity should or should not improve learning in high school science have rarely been examined together. This critical narrative review synthesises theoretical and empirical literature on iPad-assisted and closely related tablet-assisted learning strategies for students in the upper years of secondary schooling. Literature was identified through structured searches of education-specific and multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, institutional repositories and citation tracking, and was appraised for relevance, design quality and theoretical contribution. The review examines how cognitive load and multimedia learning theory, embodied cognition, inquiry-based and constructivist perspectives, sociocultural and instrumental accounts, generative learning and motivational theory explain the effects of specific strategies, and how integration frameworks such as technological pedagogical content knowledge and the substitution, augmentation, modification and redefinition model have been used, and misused, to guide practice. Strategy-level evidence is strongest for tablets used as experimental tools with multiple linked representations, for well-guided simulations and augmented visualisations, and for student-led or collaborative uses rather than teacher-led display. Meta-analytic averages are generally positive but highly heterogeneous, and they rest heavily on short, small, non-randomised and media-comparison designs, frequently outside the high school age range. Classroom studies repeatedly show that devices are mostly used to replicate existing practice, that teachers' pedagogical knowledge and beliefs condition outcomes, and that distraction, screen-based reading and unequal access remain unresolved concerns. The review proposes an integrative framework in which device affordances influence learning only through specific cognitive, social and motivational mechanisms that are activated by task design, guidance and teacher knowledge. It concludes that the decisive variable is the learning strategy rather than the device, and identifies priorities for theory-testing, longer-term and context-sensitive research.

Egypt's fertilizer industry is a major component of the petrochemical sector and relies heavily on ammonia during nitrogenous fertilizer production, creating potential occupational exposure risks for workers. Over the past decade, sustainable technological interventions and pollution-control measures have been implemented to reduce ammonia emissions and improve workplace safety. This study assessed occupational ammonia exposure among workers in a modern nitrogenous fertilizer plant in Alexandria, Egypt, and evaluated the effectiveness of these interventions. Ammonia concentrations were measured at representative operational stations using a MIRAN gas analyzer, and a structured questionnaire was administered to assess workers' occupational characteristics, use of personal protective equipment, health complaints, and awareness of occupational hazards. Ammonia concentrations ranged from 0.70 to 1.06 ppm, remaining approximately 95.8–97.2% below the occupational exposure limit of 25 ppm recommended by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). These low exposure levels were completed through the implementation of cleaner production technologies, including the Uhde ammonia synthesis process, replacement of conventional urea melting and prilling with environmentally friendly granulation technology, acidic scrubbing systems, condensate stripping, ammonia recovery and recycling, emission capture systems, and preventive maintenance practices. The findings demonstrate that integrating cleaner production technologies, Best Available Techniques (BAT), continuous environmental monitoring, ammonia detection systems, emergency response measures, and targeted occupational health training can effectively minimize occupational ammonia exposure, enhance worker safety, ensure compliance with international occupational health standards, and promote environmentally sustainable and economically efficient fertilizer production
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Technology, including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is changing professional work, but its implications for how occupational personality requirements are rewarded in the labor market remain unclear. Using job-incumbent ratings from the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (O*NET), we identify two personality requirement composites: intellectual tenacity (achievement/effort, persistence, initiative, analytical thinking, innovation, and independence) and social adjustment (emotion regulation, concern for others, social orientation, cooperation, and stress tolerance). We link these measures to more than 15 million workers in the American Community Survey from 2006 to 2024. Intellectual tenacity requirements were positively associated with hourly wages, whereas social adjustment requirements had a weaker, negative association. The wage premium for intellectual tenacity requirements was approximately stable through 2014 and rose thereafter, while the return to social adjustment requirements declined. These divergent trends began before widespread GenAI adoption, but they are concentrated in occupations with greater exposure to GenAI: wage returns for intellectual tenacity requirements increased in occupations highly exposed to GenAI, while returns to social adjustment requirements decreased in those occupations. These findings suggest that broad measures of personality or non-cognitive occupational requirements can obscure opposing shifts in the labor-market value of persistent analytical effort and social adjustment.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: This exploratory research paper proposes Interoperable Provenance Contribution (IPC), a candidate application profile grounded in W3C PROV for tracing human, AI, software and data contributions across systems. It presents six candidate evidentiary requirements, a preliminary event model, a comparison with existing technical standards and three synthetic research cases. Version 2.3, 31 October 2026. Not peer reviewed. Production interoperability and independent conformance have not yet been validated. Companion Research Materials Interactive demonstration: https://huggingface.co/spaces/GBSNResearch/ipc-provenance-explorer GitHub repository (source code and synthetic datasets): https://github.com/gbsn-research/IPC-Interoperable-Contribution-Provenance Zenodo research archive: https://zenodo.org/records/24281403 These materials illustrate the proposed IPC event representation and contribution-traceability model using synthetic examples. They do not establish production-grade provenance capture or independently validated cross-platform interoperability.

Software engineering courses are starting to ask students to build entire systems with AI coding agents, but little is known about what students actually do with them and whether they still own what they deliver. If the agent writes both the code and the decisions behind it, the artifacts we grade no longer show what students learned. We studied an assignment in which 18 pairs of students built applications with agents under Spec-Driven Development, combining the mined history of their repositories, the prompts they recorded, and a survey of 33 students. The agents wrote 69\% of the specifications meant to keep students in control, sometimes from a prompt of a few words. Students locate their ownership in the ideas, crediting themselves with half of them but a fifth of the code, yet most could not explain that code to a colleague or modify it without the agent, and what they report having written is unrelated to what their own commits declare. The three teams that met the 100,000-line target did so with generated code the application never uses, in one case proposed by the agent itself, and one team rewrote its history to backdate its specifications. Teaching with agents should therefore assess what students specify, review, and can explain, rather than what they ship, and enforce the engineering process with tools rather than trusting it to students or agents.

Whether a stored memory helps answer a user's question often depends on world knowledge rather than surface similarity. Jetriever replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring: given a query, it uses Jev, an LLM-derived System One decision model, to score every stored memory for the probability that it is useful to the answer, ranking the memory pool directly by those probabilities. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM with user-turn indexing) and reaches 76.0% end-to-end Application, compared with at most 16.0% across published retrieval and memory systems. A controlled 20-question comparison disentangles recognizing implicit evidence from ranking it properly: Jev and Qwen3.5-9B both recover 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 (versus 30% for the BERT-based decision model Laya), yet at rank 1 Jev reaches 85% while Qwen3.5-9B drops to 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever raises the four-dimension average from 44.3% (ReFind) to 55.4%, at a mean retrieval cost of USD 0.00834 per InMind query and USD 0.03103 per MAB query. Together, these results show that effective utility retrieval hinges on combining broad world knowledge, calibrated ranking probabilities, and affordable full-pool evaluation.

Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter presents a sociotechnical analysis of k-nearest neighbours (kNN) algorithm, following the same diagrammatic method. First, the description of statistical formulation and operational logic of kNN is introduced. Then, historical genealogy is presented, tracing the lineage of kNN back to nearest neighbour rule in optics and heuristics (Occam’s Razor), as well as connecting this lineage to sociological research on homophily and the spatial logic of difference. The chapter argues that as an operational diagram kNN modulates differences through organizing them into partitions based on relations of similarity and dis/connection, while materializing homophilic principles of sociality and segregation that permeate network science.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Based on 30 named individual cases documented in public media reports, this paper analyzes the knowledge structure, transmission pathways and talent development challenges associated with Atlas Silk craftsmanship from a human resource management perspective. The B1-B11 framework is used to summarize knowledge content and training arrangements, and the C1-C10 framework is used to identify training, retention and job support issues. The results show that the process and material knowledge can be incorporated into structured training, and the embodied experience of warping, dyeing and weaving still depends on long-term field practice. Families, workshops, cooperatives, colleges and digital communication have complementary functions. To support talent succession, we should combine the phased ability development, compensation guarantee, whole process rotation, dual-mentor training and work design that takes into account the family situation. This paper is a purposively selected literature-based case study, which is not statistically representative.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.

Speech language models (SLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and general-purpose speech understanding, yet ASR-specific training often degrades spoken question answering (QA) performance. We revisit this conflict from the perspective of task-specific input--output mappings and one-hot supervision. Our findings reveal pronounced task-asymmetric effects: ASR-only training severely limits QA capability, whereas QA-only training retains reasonable ASR performance. We hypothesize that the relatively deterministic mapping of ASR, combined with single-reference supervision, biases models toward transcription-specific behavior. Motivated by this perspective, we advocate broadening ASR learning objectives while preserving recognition accuracy. We propose Learning from Distribution (LFD), which aligns speech-conditioned predictions with the conditional output distributions of a pretrained text LLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFD improves both ASR and QA performance, exhibits superior data efficiency, and remains effective under full-parameter fine-tuning. CoT-ASR further supports the broader applicability of our proposed supervision principle.

LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks where they must explore, gather experience, and adapt their decisions accordingly. We name this capability in-context adaptivity: improving decisions across episodes from experience accumulated in context. We propose to evaluate it in repeated imperfect-information games against unknown opponents. In these games, fixed game-theoretically optimal policies cannot achieve maximum reward, whereas adapting to the opponent increases returns across games. We design a paired protocol that evaluates each agent with and without memory under identical conditions to isolate experience gain from single-game skill. Evaluation shows that memory brings little performance gain for open-weight models and inconsistent gains for frontier models. Our analysis of the agents' summaries and actions identifies a memory-doing gap in which models accurately record opponent tendencies yet rarely depart from default play. To close this gap, we construct a pool of exploitable opponents and post-train Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. We optimize full-match return across context segments so summary generation and action selection are trained together. On unseen opponents, our 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over supervised fine-tuning in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em. Across 35 opponents, our policy matches or surpasses frontier models, generalizes beyond its training horizon, and retains most of its gain on summaries from frontier models.

Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.

Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.

Chapter 3 presents a sociotechnical analysis of linear regression as an operational diagram. It introduces the logical and statistical formulation of linear regression and delves into the history of this method, particularly its conceptualization by Francis Galton, connecting this history to the notions of normality and averages in statistics. The entanglements of the conception of normality and Galton’s work with eugenics are explored. The chapter connects this historical context and the workings of linear regression as an operational diagram by presenting an argument that linear regression in its operations and through its historical, primarily eugenics-oriented contexts actualizes the norming linear thinking by constructing the line of best fit, defining difference in relation to the norm.
topics: Philosophy of Biology and Scientific Explanation

documents.abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.

Service robots in ambient intelligence (AmI) scenarios such as smart factories and home services must rapidly adapt to diverse manipulation tasks, yet traditional reinforcement learning (RL) reward design heavily relies on domain expertise, requiring days to weeks of manual tuning. Existing LLM-assisted reward design methods assume that generated rewards can be directly applied to training environments, overlooking potential incompatibility with built-in training mechanisms such as curriculum learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the signal interference phenomenon between LLM-generated rewards and curriculum dynamic weight adjustments---experiments reveal that curriculum modules amplify penalty weights from an initial $-1\times10^{-4}$ to $-0.1$ (a factor of 1000$\times$), overwhelming the positive reward signals---and it proposes an automatic detection and correction mechanism based on feedback ratio anomaly detection. A unified dual-paradigm framework adapting to both ManagerBasedRL and DirectRL paradigms on the IsaacLab platform, along with a humanized interaction paradigm for non-expert users, are also developed. Systematic experiments on five robot tasks of varying difficulty, including ablation studies, 8-sample random search baselines, and multi-seed statistical tests, demonstrate: on Franka Lift the success rate increases from 0\% to 84\%$\pm$2\% and the mean reward from 0.90 to 84.41$\pm$5.50, where simply disabling the curriculum yields a roughly 5$\times$ increase in mean reward (0.90$\rightarrow$4.47)---a necessary prerequisite for LLM reward optimization to take effect---and combining it with the LLM-designed multi-stage reward structure multiplies the improvement by a further 18.9$\times$; under an equal-compute random-search comparison, LLM weight optimization achieves a 47\% improvement over the best random configuration. Mean-reward ratios depend on the reward definition and should be read together with the scale-invariant success rate. The method reduces reward design time from expert-days to hours, validated on the commercial LLM DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

In recent years, Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) methods driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance in decision interpretability and environmental transferability, yet suffer from low decision efficiency and unstable decision-making. To mitigate these limitations, this work proposes a multi-agent hybrid LLM–expert system framework for ACD. The framework seamlessly integrates the determinism and efficiency of expert systems with the deep reasoning capabilities of LLMs: the expert system makes deterministic decisions based on experiential knowledge, whereas the LLM is responsible for complex decision tasks demanding deep exploration and long-chain reasoning. We further strengthen the LLM via chain-of-thought (CoT) guided prompting, historical memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), output alignment and feedback learning. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the expert system improves both decision efficiency and defense performance. Evaluated on the CybORG CC4 environment, our approach achieves an average reward of − 98 over ten independent rounds, representing an approximate 25.5% improvement over the best-performing reinforcement learning (RL) baseline. Compared with the standalone LLM method, the average reward increases by roughly 96.2%, while the average per-step runtime is reduced by approximately 14.6%. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically integrate LLMs and expert systems for ACD in the CybORG CC4 environment.

Web 3.0 represents the next generation of the Internet, which is widely recognized as a decentralized ecosystem that focuses on value expression and data ownership. By leveraging blockchain and artificial intelligence technologies, Web 3.0 offers unprecedented opportunities for users to create, own, and monetize their content, thereby enabling User-Generated Content (UGC) to an entirely new level. However, self-interested users may exploit the limitations of content curation mechanisms and generate low-quality content with less effort, obtaining platform rewards under information asymmetry. Such behavior can undermine Web 3.0 performance. To this end, we propose LMM-Incentive , a novel Large Multimodal Model (LMM)-based incentive mechanism for UGC in Web 3.0. Specifically, we propose an LMM-based contract-theoretic model to motivate users to generate high-quality UGC, thereby mitigating the adverse selection problem from information asymmetry. To alleviate potential moral hazards after contract selection, we leverage LMM agents to evaluate UGC quality, which is the primary component of the contract, utilizing prompt engineering techniques to improve the evaluation performance of LMM agents. Recognizing that traditional contract design methods cannot effectively adapt to the dynamic environment of Web 3.0, we develop an improved Mixture of Experts (MoE)-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm for optimal contract design. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed MoE-based PPO algorithm over representative benchmarks in the context of contract design, where the proposed algorithm achieves a \(5.4\%\) improvement in test rewards over the PPO algorithm. Finally, we deploy the designed contract within an Ethereum smart contract framework, further validating the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

Recent advances in foundation models have enabled robotic agents to reason, plan, and adapt their actions through physical interaction. Yet successful execution does not necessarily translate into lasting improvement across tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising paradigm for robotic agents to continuously refine their capabilities through experience, but requires preserving functional knowledge, adapting execution to changing physical conditions, and retaining reusable corrections. We introduce LoopROS, a dual-loop robotic agent framework that couples functionally constrained execution with experience-driven improvement. Within each episode, functional constraint-guided in-context learning identifies essential task relations from demonstrations and context, while visual feedback-guided segmentwise trajectory tuning adapts reference motions through observation-grounded corrections and verification. Across episodes, execution feedback informs revisions to persistent skills, parameters, and executable tools, enabling subsequent executions to reuse corrections under relevant conditions. The LoopROS achieves an 82.0% success rate and a mean score of 88.90, ranking No. 1 in RoboDojo, among the compared methods. We further complete 30 successful trials in three real robot manipulation tasks, elucidating its great potential as a backbone robotic RSI.

As mixed reality (MR) systems enter everyday environments, interacting while lying down is an emerging design context. However, existing research has largely focused on supine configurations, overlooking the asymmetric constraints of lateral postures and their interplay with input modality. To address this gap, we conducted a 3 × 2 within-subjects study (N = 36) evaluating pointing performance across three recumbent postures (Supine, Dominant, NonDominant) and two input modalities (Controller and Hand raycasting). Results show that posture effects are strongly moderated by modality: while controller input remained stable, hand input degraded substantially in lateral postures. Furthermore, supported-arm postures increased wrist-rotation demands, whereas unsupported-arm postures led to higher perceived exertion. These findings highlight how posture and modality jointly shape performance and ergonomic burden, informing design considerations for posture-aware recumbent MR interfaces.

Multimodal graphs integrate textual and visual attributes with relational structures, providing a rich representation of complex real-world data. To enable the broad applicability and reuse of graph models, it is crucial for models trained on source graphs to generalize to unseen graph domains. However, this is challenging because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. This gives rise to two key challenges: adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variations across nodes and domains; and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information needed for each target node to support LLM-based prediction. In light of these challenges, we propose MAGE (Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting), a framework for transferable multimodal graph learning. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components. Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation (MAMP) adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning (EGIT) selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal LLM. Together, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates. Experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs demonstrate strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, without requiring parameter updates on the target domains.

Workers in firefighting, emergency response, aviation, welding, metal processing, and petrochemical operations may be exposed to flame, radiant or convective heat, hot surfaces, molten materials, smoke, and chemical contaminants. Fire-protective clothing is needed when these hazards cannot be fully controlled at source. However, dense multilayer assemblies and chemical treatments can limit heat and moisture loss, increase cardiovascular and metabolic strain, restrict movement, and make cleaning and disposal more difficult. This critical narrative review focuses on structural firefighting and examines research on protective materials, garment engineering, occupational hygiene, ergonomics, thermophysiology, maintenance, and life-cycle management. Studies were selected purposively through a targeted literature update and synthesized across heterogeneous methods and endpoints. Flame resistance at the material level is only one determinant of protection in use. Outcomes also depend on the complete ensemble, wearer, task, environment, and service history. Added insulation can slow external heat transfer while limiting dissipation of metabolic heat; cleaning can remove contaminants but reduce mechanical, barrier, or heat-loss performance; and renewable or recycled content may have limited value if it shortens service life or creates additional chemical and recovery problems. The review proposes a two-stage evaluation approach: first, apply minimum safety requirements that cannot be offset by benefits in other domains; second, compare compliant systems in terms of physiological load, mobility, chemical safety, durability, maintainability, cost, and environmental effects. The synthesis informs condition-based inspection, validated decontamination, representative wear trials, worker input, chemical disclosure, and product-level service records. The framework and proposed service-based sustainability measure require prospective validation; laboratory performance and acute wearer responses do not establish reduced injury or disease incidence.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Explanations of machine learning models are read by people but rarely evaluated with them, and automatic metrics score attribution vectors rather than what a reader receives. We operationalise the horizon, the hermeneutic circle, and the hermeneutics of suspicion as the Hermeneutic Circle Test (HCT), a human-free screen for explanations of tabular classifiers. HCT checks whether an explanation’s evidence lies inside a calibrated data horizon, whether its sentences survive on-horizon interventions, whether its account of a case agrees with the whole model and at which scale, and whether it helps machine readers learn the model. Over seven explainers, four datasets, and two model families (mean ± standard deviation over eight settings), the best explainer, KernelSHAP, verified 0.65 ± 0.15 of its claims, while random attributions verified 0.22 ± 0.08. On the same explanations, established faithfulness, remove-and-retrain, and disagreement metrics missed impossible evidence and narratives contradicting their own attributions, and sign-blind metrics scored sign-flipped explanations like the originals. Claim tests withstood scaffold attacks that adapt to the horizon and to the test itself; a scaffold that memorises the audited records weakened them and deceived every explainer, but part–whole agreement still flagged it. HCT is a reproducible screen to apply before user studies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.

This study examines the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on employee performance in selected Federal Teaching Hospitals and Federal Medical Centres in Nigeria, with a focus on the mediating role of AI-Human Collaboration. A cross-sectional research design was adopted. The population comprised clinical and non-clinical healthcare workers in selected public healthcare institutions in Nigeria. Using a multistage sampling technique 520 questionnaires were distributed, of which 371 valid responses were analyzed. SmartPLS 4 was employed for data analysis. Findings reveal that AI adoption significantly enhances both AIhuman collaboration and employee performance. AI-human collaboration also has a significant positive effect on employee performance and significantly mediates the relationship between AI adoption and employee performance. The study concludes that AI adoption improves employee performance both directly and indirectly through enhanced collaboration between employees and AI systems. It recommends that healthcare institutions should strengthen AI-human collaboration through continuous training and integration of AI technologies to maximize performance outcomes. These measures are essential for improving workforce efficiency and achieving sustainable performance in Nigeria’s healthcare sector.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.

The article presents methodological approaches to conducting forensic examination of occupational health and safety which, in turn, are based on a systemic-activity approach and consist of a sequence of interrelated stages aimed at establishing the causes, circumstances, and consequences of accidents and incidents. The purpose of using them is to ensure the comprehensiveness, objectivity, and reproducibility of the expert examination, as well as its focus on preventing similar incidents in the future.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence chatbots increasingly advise farmers, yet their adoption should rest on rigorous, standardised evaluation. This review brings together five standardised instruments for assessing chatbots (the System Usability Scale, the Chatbot Usability Scale, the Checklist for Trust between People and Automation, the AI Chatbots Usage Scale, and the User Engagement Scale) and one assessment method, knowledge testing. It also explains Cronbach’s alpha, the reliability criterion most of them rely on. A case study from the literature, in which five large language models answered PhD-level soil science questions, together with deployed systems such as Farmer.Chat and AgroLLM, show how evaluation works in practice and why fluent but unverified advice is risky. Beyond questionnaires, we examine accuracy-based and retrieval-grounded testing. We propose a five-layer protocol that first checks technical accuracy, then usability, trust, engagement, and learning outcomes, to guide the design and validation of chatbots for precision and smallholder farming.

Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at https://github.com/minhquoc0712/BECON.

In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

The cognitive burden associated with upper-limb prosthesis use remains a barrier to functional adoption, yet existing evaluations often rely on single-modality measures. This study investigates a multimodal framework for assessing cognitive load during activities of daily living. Twelve participants without limb loss performed standardized activities of daily living using their natural hand and a simulated tendon-driven prosthesis in a within-subject design. This controlled baseline was used to evaluate modality-specific responses to prosthesis-mediated task demands across subjective, behavioral, and neurophysiological measures. Cognitive workload was assessed using task performance metrics, subjective ratings from the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), eye-tracking measures including gaze behavior and pupillary dynamics, and prefrontal cortical activation measured with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Prosthesis use increased NASA-TLX mental demand by 2.80–3.85 points across tasks (all p < 0.001) and prefrontal oxygenated hemoglobin by 0.96–1.14 μ M across regions during carton transfer and pour (all p < 0.001). Pupillary activity differentiated conditions during block transfer ( p < 0.001) and checker transfer ( p < 0.05), but not carton transfer and pour ( p = 0.47), demonstrating task-dependent responses across modalities. A multimodal framework provides a more comprehensive assessment of cognitive load than any single measure alone, offering valuable insights into how cognitive demand manifests across behavioral, perceptual, and biological domains. This framework establishes a controlled baseline for multimodal cognitive workload assessment and provides a foundation for future investigations in individuals with limb loss.

Situation awareness (SA) in disaster management requires robust modeling of multimodal big data from complex environments. With the increasing availability of large-scale video and audio data from surveillance systems, drones, and public sensors, multimodal approaches have become essential for improving reliability. However, existing methods often rely on uniform data sampling and treat modalities equally, limiting their effectiveness when data quality varies across time and modality. Compared with our previous work, this study extends from modality-specific analysis to a multimodal audio–visual framework. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MSA-SD², a multimodal situation awareness framework specifically designed for big data environments based on selective dual self-distillation. An adaptive temporal sampling and alignment module is introduced to prioritize informative temporal segments and ensure consistent audio–visual correspondence, enabling efficient processing of large-scale multimodal big data. For visual representation, a superpixels-guided vision transformer is employed, while a transformer-based audio encoder models temporal acoustic patterns. A multimodal student model is guided by visual and audio teacher models through a selective distillation strategy that adapts to modality reliability. Experimental results demonstrate improved performance on large-scale multimodal datasets, particularly under challenging big data conditions with varying data quality across modalities.

In-vehicle alerts can support timely responses to hazards, but their sensory and informational demands may also produce annoyance and perceived overload. This scoping review mapped physiological, neurocognitive, and psychophysiological processes investigated or proposed in relation to these responses. Searches in Scopus, APA PsycINFO, and PubMed identified 1,304 records; 955 remained after deduplication, and 16 studies were included in the final synthesis. The synthesis distinguished subjective experiences, physiological indicators, behavioral outcomes, and explanatory mechanisms. Attentional competition, working memory capacity, warning complexity, and presentation timing were relevant to processing demands. Multimodal alerts supported detection and response under some conditions, while also presenting potential costs in startle and intrusiveness. Heart rate variability and electrodermal activity were sensitive to task demands and risk-related arousal, but did not independently identify irritation. Heterogeneity and the absence of formal risk-of-bias assessment limited causal and design conclusions. Future research should combine subjective, physiological, and behavioral measures, separate warning effects from concurrent task and hazard effects, and evaluate repeated exposure and adaptive interfaces in naturalistic driving. Warning assessment should therefore consider tolerability and processing costs alongside response performance.

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.

Human resource development in the modern era emphasizes not only professional knowledge and work performance but also workplace safety as a fundamental factor for organizational sustainability. This academic article aims to analyze the principles of human resource development based on workplace safety concepts, focusing on situation awareness and effective decision-making in reducing work-related risks and enhancing organizational development. The analysis indicates that personnel equipped with safety knowledge, situational awareness, and analytical skills are more capable of making appropriate decisions, minimizing human errors, and promoting life and workplace safety. Furthermore, recognizing people as the key mechanism of organizational development contributes to the establishment of a strong safety culture that supports work efficiency, collaboration, and sustainable organizational growth. Therefore, human resource development under workplace safety principles is essential.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Background Occupational hazards remain a substantial concern in the non-ferrous metal mining and processing industry. Using Guangxi’s abundant non-ferrous mineral resources, this study analyzed workplace occupational-hazard monitoring and occupational health examination data to support evidence-based prevention and control of occupational diseases in the region. Methods Using data from the monitoring system for 2021–2025, we conducted descriptive analyses of workplace occupational hazards and applied multivariable logistic regression models to identify factors associated with workers’ abnormal pulmonary function and high-frequency hearing loss. Results Between 2021 and 2025, a total of 306 enterprises and 2,379 positions were monitored. Noise showed the highest cumulative exceedance rate (33.1%), followed by dust (11.7%; C TWA exceedance of 20.0% for silica dust versus 1.2% for other dust) and lead (1.3%). Over the five-year period, workers’ exposure rates to all hazardous agents declined consistently (all p for trend < 0.001), and the silica dust exceedance rate also decreased. Among 16,213 examined workers (mean age 43.5 years; 83.2% male), the detection rate of abnormal pulmonary function was 8.7% and that of high-frequency hearing loss was 18.8%; the detection rate of hearing loss increased progressively over the years before declining in 2025. Multivariable logistic regression showed that male sex and older age were associated with both outcomes. Workers in state-owned and private enterprises had higher odds of abnormal pulmonary function (OR = 2.20 and 2.61, respectively), and the odds increased with enterprise size (OR = 1.77–2.48). For high-frequency hearing loss, workers with ≥10 years of service (OR = 1.15) and those employed in rock drilling, transportation, and flotation positions had significantly elevated odds (OR = 4.71, 2.81, and 1.91, respectively). Conclusion Supervision of noise and dust must be continuously strengthened, particularly in micro-enterprises. Optimizing engineering controls and raising awareness of personal protection are essential for reducing the risk of occupational diseases.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Environmental Health Practitioners (EHPs) undertake regulatory, inspection and field-based activities that may expose them to multiple occupational hazards. Although personal protective equipment (PPE) is an important occupational risk-control measure, evidence concerning its effectiveness specifically among EHPs remains limited. The study aims to synthesise and evaluate available evidence on occupational hazards and the effectiveness of PPE interventions relevant to EHPs working in government regulatory services. A systematic review was conducted and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Various Research platforms were searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2000 and March 2026. Studies involving EHPs and related regulatory professionals were included, together with relevant evidence from comparable occupational groups where the hazards, exposure pathways or PPE interventions applied to environmental health practice. Due to heterogeneity in study designs, populations, PPE interventions and outcomes, findings were synthesised narratively. Thirty-four unique studies were included. Biological hazards were most frequently reported (82.4%), followed by chemical (47.1%), physical (44.1%), psychosocial (32.4%), organisational/workplace (26.5%), climate/environmental (17.6%) and radiation hazards (2.9%). Respiratory protection was the most frequently reported PPE category (70.6%), followed by gloves (55.9%), protective clothing (41.2%), eye/face protection (35.3%) and protective footwear (20.6%). Overall, appropriately selected PPE reduced occupational exposure; however, effectiveness varied by PPE type and occupational context and was influenced by availability, training, knowledge, adherence, comfort, correct donning and doffing, contamination control, and organisational support. Of the 34 studies, only three directly investigated EHPs, Environmental Health Officers, or Public Health Inspectors. PPE is an important component of occupational protection for EHPs but should be selected according to the specific hazard, task and exposure route and implemented within a broader occupational risk-management approach. The limited direct evidence among environmental health regulatory professionals highlights the need for EHP-specific research to inform PPE guidelines, training and occupational health policies.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

AI complicates both decisions because it changes the work learners can produce and what that work reveals about learning.
