documents.abstract: Assembling objects in Virtual Reality using hand actions is cognitively demanding because users must identify relationships among components. We present Spatial Visual Guides (SVG), a novel user interface that provides context-sensitive visual guides designed to scaffold users’ spatial reasoning during 3D assembly tasks. Users invoke SVG automatically through naturalistic hand actions (Hand-SVG) or deliberately through a multimodal combination of voice and hand input (VoiceHand-SVG). In a user study, 24 participants performed a 3D assembly task at two levels of complexity (easy and hard) using SVG. We found a difference in usage between the multimodal VoiceHand-SVG interface and Hand-SVG: VoiceHand-SVG produced fewer guide activations while remaining visible for similar durations. Moreover, participants’ articulated strategies and behavioural logs helped us understand how participants used SVGs during assembly, and showed that participants used SVGs for orientation anchoring, relational comparison, and placement planning. SVGs also improved task performance compared to no visual feedback. Our results demonstrate the advantages of designing visual guides around specific spatial reasoning behaviours, and reveal trade-offs between unimodal and multimodal interaction strategies.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

Purpose This study aims to investigate the strategic futures of business-to-business (B2B) marketing by identifying the interlinked themes shaping its transformation, with particular attention to artificial intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting force embedded in sociotechnical and institutional developments. Design/methodology/approach A two-round Delphi study with 29C-level industry experts was conducted. Responses were coded into 192 thematic mentions across 16 themes, analyzed through co-occurrence mapping and classified in a dual-axis typology by perceived nature (opportunity vs challenge) and origin (sociotechnical vs institutional). Findings AI is central but rarely operates in isolation: it co-occurs with every other theme, functioning as the connective node between internal capabilities and external demands in interorganizational relationships. The typology reveals a statistically significant attribution asymmetry (χ2(1) = 40.23, p < 0.001): internally buildable themes are framed as opportunities, externally imposed demands as challenges. Originality/value The paper theorizes AI not as a tool within the firm but as a boundary-spanning coordination mechanism coupling sociotechnical and institutional domains. The dual-axis typology, tested attribution asymmetry and three propositions provide a foresight-driven framework for understanding strategic readiness in B2B transformation.
